articles.description:
Creativity doesn’t drive my blogging; software does. So daily.baty.net is back in rotation and is once again built using Tinderbox.
Tinderbox is special. I've been preaching this for more than 20 years. However, my use of Tinderbox has slowed down in recent years due to the distraction that is Linux. I felt I needed to move away from macOS-only software. I shouldn't have.
I've been "going ham" with Tinderbox recently, and it feels good. I used to live in its Map views, but that was back when I was working. Now, I use it mostly as a fancy outliner (it's a really good outliner) and as a blogging tool.
Tinderbox manages daily.baty.net. For a minute I was using Eleventy, but no longer. Tinderbox's export features are complex, and sometimes I get lost, but they're also very flexible and powerful.
Long story short, when I'm experiencing the rush that comes with rediscovering Tinderbox, I want to use it for everything, so I brought it back and I'm posting daily notes there instead of journal entries here.
In case you were wondering.
✍️ Reply by email

articles.description:
org-capture and then create a note1 while the
capture is active (as I'm doing now), you might be very surprised
when you press C-c C-c to finish the note -- it vanishes!
Don't Panic!
In order to see the note, you'll need to press C-c C-c a second time
to complete the capture.  Then org-capture adds the item into the
Org file, along with the note.

My preference in this situation is to write only the first phrase
  or sentence of the note.  Then I issue the two presses of C-c
    C-c and complete the note at its destination.  I do this
  not only to avoid the "scary missing note" scenario; I also worry
  about leaving work unsaved for any amount of time.  The computers I
  grew up with were prone to crashing at inopportune times, so I
  adopted the motto, "Save Early; save often."  An Org note is
  composed in the *Org Note* buffer, which has no file associated
  with it and therefore is not a good candidate for saving.
1 With C-c C-z (org-add-note)

articles.description:
the release of Journelly 1.5. It’s the formal release of the beta version that I recently wrote about. I can’t say enough about this release. As I’ve said before, my Journelly database is over 4 thousand entries long and before this release Journelly was getting laggy and hard to use but this release resolved all those problems. Now Journelly is as snappy as it was when I had only a few entries and everything about it seems faster and easier.


But wait. There’s more. Ramírez has added an “on this day” feature as well as adding features that make searching for entries by date easier.


If you use Journelly as a journal, you may be interested in the new “on this day” feature. There’s a new button that will show you entries happening on the same day from other years. My particular use case for Journelly is as a memo book so I have no use for this feature. Fortunately, the new Journelly makes it easy to toggle it off if you don’t want it.


The other new significant feature is enhanced searching by date. In the search function you can use on: keyword with several different date formats to search for entries with a particular date. There’s also a calendar button that lets you choose the date from a calendar presentation if you prefer.


You may wonder why I have this entry tagged emacs. I consider Journelly intrinsically linked with Emacs because Journelly keeps its database in an Org file and that means that I can use Emacs and Org mode to search and edit that database. That doesn’t seem like much but I find myself doing it all the time. Journelly has become integrated into my Emacs workflow and become an important part of it.


In the mean time, those of you not in the Journelly beta program now have access to these updates. I can’t speak for Ramírez, of course, but if you’d like to be in the beta program, email Ramírez. He’ll probably be glad to add you.

The Emacs Carnival topic for November is: Discovery of Emacs Features.
How I Discover Features
My biggest new feature discovery method is Emacs News. Normally I'll clear every other item out of my RSS feeds and then dedicate a single reading session to reading Emacs News because I open up so many links to read that it needs its own dedicated session.
Being fairly new in my Emacs journey I find new interesting features all the time, my biggest issue is the time to add them to me workflows. I've been in Emacs long enough now that I dream of being able to move most of my work into it. I open Obsidian to write and wonder why I'm not writing in Emacs. I have Kitty open and wonder why I don't just use Emacs?
There is so much to learn in Emacs, and so many things  it could replace I'm sort of stuck wondering where to even start.

articles.description: When I customize my Emacs, I often utilize hooks. However, when experimenting, I often inadvertently add the wrong thing to a hook – a function I later decide to rename or even a lambda. I have always painstakingly written the correct remove-hook invocation to do it. A few days ago it occurred to me that it would be nice to write an interactive wrapper around remove-hook to make it easier. As usual in such cases, I started with a bit of research to see if someone did something similar already. To my surprise, not only is this a solved problem, but it’s solved in Emacs itself! Apparently, almost six years ago remove-hook was made into a command and you can just M-x it, provide the hook variable name and use autocompletion to decide what to remove from it (including lambdas!). How cool is that?
articles.title: Marcin Borkowski: A tip on removing functions from hooks interactively

articles.description:
Org mode is often celebrated for its ability to “write once, export anywhere.”
With such power comes added complexity: Exporting a file requires the user to typically go through a multi-step process (e.g. C-c C-e <some char> <some other char>). If the user is concerned with previewing changes to their file, then another step of viewing the exported output is required. Having to do this repeatedly gets tedious fast. Such is the motivation for Burnish.
Burnish is a new Elisp package I’ve made to automate the export and viewing of an Org file. It provides an Emacs minor mode (burnish-mode) that when enabled, does the following upon save of an Org file:
Export the Org file to a specified export backend.
View the exported output in another Emacs window or by external tool.
Most all of the default backends provided by Org mode are supported by Burnish. That said, Burnish is highly configurable, allowing for users to define for themselves the export and view workflow for existing or third party backends.
Read the Burnish User Guide to learn more about it. As it is new, feedback is always welcome. If you really find it useful, please show your gratitude by buying me a coffee.
Burnish v1.0 is now available on MELPA.
articles.title: Charles Choi: Announcing Burnish

articles.description:
After last night’s post, I realised I was probably just getting too invested in somehow using imdb for the “who’s that actor, anyway?” command for my Emacs-based video player.
Not only is it an extremely fragile setup that’s gonna stop working, but it’s also very slow — it takes half a minute to return the actor profile images.
So I just implemented a tmdb API shim and then I ask it for the actor profile photo instead.  tmdb doesn’t have as large a data base, but…  The API is free (for non-commercial use) and is extremely easy to use.
Things are now faster:

The main wait is from the response from the LLM — I’m using gemini-3.8-flash.  I’ve tried gemini-3.1-flash-lite, and it’s much faster…  but gives the wrong result most of the time.  No, that’s not Roy Scheider, Gemini!
So now the setup is less Rube Goldberguesque.  Sort of:
I hit a key on my li’l wireless keyboard.

It’s picked up by a Python script that listens for evdev events.

It uses emacsclient to notify the Emacs running on the TV machine.

Emacs there tells mpv to do a screenshot.

Emacs waits until the screenshot arrives on disc.

Emacs sends it to Gemini and says “who dis? JSON please”.

Gemini responds and Emacs then creates an SVG overlay with the actor name.

rsvg-convert converts to PNG and then imagemagick convert to BGRA.

Emacs asks mpv to display it.

Emacs asks tmdb for the actor profile URL and fetches the image.

If it gets a response, it then recreates the svg with the image embedded.

(repeat 8-9).

Couldn’t be simpler.
articles.title: Lars Ingebrigtsen: OK, OK, I’ll just use tmdb

articles.description:
interesting post about BYOK. BYOK is a “writer deck”, a device exclusively for writing that has no distracting apps or even a connection to the Internet. The idea is that writers can’t get distracted when they reach a temporary block by escaping to social media or something similar; they have to push through the block and get on with their writing.


According to Martin, BYOK is better than most devices in its class but there are still problems. He doesn’t like the available fonts and the screen—as you can see from the picture in his post—is pretty small, about 6 lines depending on the font. That seems to me to amount to a rather uncomfortable working environment. Fortunately, I don’t usually find myself distracted when I’m writing.


Then there’s the matter of research. Very often you need to look something up when you’re writing and you can’t do that with something like BYOK so you need to switch devices,  pulling you even further out of the flow. And as Martin observes, it’s not easy to integrate your notes either.


The deal buster for me, though, is the builtin editor. It’s not Emacs based and doesn’t even support Emacs keybindings for navigation. As I’ve repeatedly said—as recently as yesterday—I simply can’t comfortably write outside of Emacs anymore. Martin is a relative newcomer to Emacs but he’s already feeling the discomfort. Once the Emacs way sets in, he’ll be just like me and won’t consider doing serious writing outside of Emacs.


Even if I were subject to being distracted by the greater Internet, I would simply turn off my WiFi to produce what is effectively an Emacs based writer deck. One thing for sure, I’m not giving up Emacs and suffering a second rate writing environment.
articles.title: Irreal: BYOK

articles.description:
And now it’s all this, Dr Drang has a post on using TextEdit versus using Pages. He’s a Mac user, obviously, but that doesn’t matter so much. The real argument is over whether one should use a word processor or some sort of text based editor.


There can be no doubt on where I stand on the issue. The only time I can remember using a “word processor” of any type in the last 3 decades was when I had to collaborate on another author’s file as a technical editor1. As I’ve said before, whenever I write in anything other than Emacs, I feel like I’m in Bizarro World where nothing works as it should. That includes even things like iMessage which is why I tend to use emacs-everywhere for it and most other things.


Dr Drang is nominally the same. He says he almost never uses a Word Processor but sometimes for a one-off he thinks it makes sense to use a word processor rather than one of his LaTeX or Markdown templates. That seems backwards to me. Sure, maybe you don’t want to use a template for a technical report to write a quick note to your baby sitter but Pages or any other word processor is not the simple alternative. I’d simply use Org and export it to whatever format seems appropriate. Even if Dr Drang is not an Emacs user, he is a Markdown user so surely the easy thing for him to do is to dash off his quick note in Markdown.


Really, unless you have collaboration issues, there’s no reason to subject yourself to the horrors of a word processor.


Footnotes: 
1 



That post was so long ago that I was still using Groff instead of Org to typeset documents. I’ve done technical editing since then that also required a Word clone and the experience was no better.
articles.title: Irreal: Why Use A Word Processor When You Have Org?

articles.description:
Journelly. I use it as my memo book to record my daily activities and random things that I want to remember. For example, if I see some article or ad in my browser, I can ask Safari to share it with Journelly and a Journelly entry is automatically made complete with a link to whatever it was I wanted to capture. Each entry contains a date/time stamp as well as the location of where the entry was made.


Best of all, Journelly keeps its data as an Org file so I can query or edit it in Emacs. Of course, Journelly has a search function but sometimes I want to do a more complicated search or even to just count the number of entries in the database (4361 as of right now). Having the database as an Org file means that my data is available on all my devices, even if that device is a Mac.


I’ve been using Journelly since March 2025, ever since it was in beta, and have never looked back. Lately, however, it’s been getting a bit laggy, something I put down to my large database. I was on the verge of truncating my active data to the most recent entries in order to improve performance when Álvaro Ramírez pushed a new beta—v1.5(4)—that completely solved the problem. Now Journelly performs just like it did when I started.


If you are an Emacs user and are using an iPhone/iPad, I can’t think of any reason why you wouldn’t want to use Journelly. It allows you to integrate your day-to-day note taking with the power of Org mode. Even if you aren’t an Emacs user, you’ll probably find Journelly useful. It can also save its data as a markdown file so you can still get all the benefits of an easily accessible and editable database even if you prefer another editor.
articles.title: Irreal: A New Journelly Beta

articles.description:
another step in the journey so many of are on: moving everything inside Emacs. Regular Irreal readers will recall that Ridenour is a Philosophy professor so he doesn’t have much need for high powered math tools but he does have to deal with grade calculations and various budget items. He had been using Soulver for this but, of course, this meant leaving Emacs, something all we Emacers hate.


Then he stumbled on literate-calc-mode. It did everything that Soulver did and Ridenour didn’t have to leave Emacs to use it. It’s been a win for him and he’s happy with it.


When I read Ridenour’s post, something seemed familiar. It turns out that I’d written about literate-calc-mode six years ago. It had just been released and no one had any experience with it yet. I meant to follow up but, of course, life intervened and I never did. I’m glad to see that it’s still around and has lived up to its potential.


I’m tempted to install it but I’m reasonably proficient with Calc itself so I probably wouldn’t use it enough to make it worthwhile. Still, if Reverse Polish Notation is not your thing and you’d rather deal with normal infix notation, literate-calc-mode may be a good fit. It’s easy to try out so give it a spin if you’re interested.
articles.title: Irreal: Ridenour On Literate Calc Mode

articles.description:
Get past the unseasoned beef between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown in Tuesday's Celtics-Sixers matchup, and reach instead for the real juice: a killer performance by Paul George, the player for whom Brown was traded. Though a single regular-season game in November is no way useful to assess a trade in its entirety, the contrast last night between those two wings was telling: Brown (keyed-up, foul-prone, poor decision-making) sat out much of a game where George (methodical, efficient, at ease in the flow of offense) flourished. Boston won, 123-101. More than anything, George's 36-point outing was a reminder of his eerily slick, timeless style could have plugged into every NBA roster constructed over the last decade, and how it distills Joe Mazzulla's Celtics squad to its spiritual essence.
Fair minds were skeptical that a star version of George would ever return. In two years with Philly, he seemed to have receded into a fog of lower-body injuries, mystery drug use, and inconsistent podcasting, playing just 78 total regular-season games. Meanwhile, Brown had just come off a workhorse campaign for the Celtics, logging 71 games while soaking up 36 percent usage on his way to an All-NBA second team. For all the hand-wringing about Brown's true value, both in a vacuum and within the Celtics system, he was clearly the more valuable player at the time of the trade. When swapping two seemingly onerous contracts for one another, each one asking somewhere between 32 and 35 percent of the salary cap for a wing who likely wouldn't live up to that price tag, it was the Sixers who had to sweeten the deal with draft picks.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d7mSyzoPfbk
articles.title: Paul George Has Turned Out To Be The Ur-Celtic

articles.description:
Three years ago, after a long but loveless marriage, the Minnesota Vikings let QB Kirk Cousins walk out the door. They felt free. Unburdened. Hopeful, even. No longer would they have to spend night after night asking themselves, “Where is this relationship going?” They could finally find someone new. They could believe in love again, and maybe even have a bit of fun getting back out there on the scene.
That scene, much to the Vikings’ chagrin, turned out to be far less exciting than they’d anticipated. Maybe it was them. Maybe they weren’t quite as charming and attractive as they thought they’d been. Regardless, they eventually found themselves lonely, broken, and frankly hard up. And so, with Taylor Swift’s “Style” playing on a loop in the background, they swallowed their pride, along with a good amount of red wine, and made the call they swore they’d never make. Kirk Cousins is a Viking again, and us Vikings fans feel a little bit ashamed that we let this happen all over again. That’s the subject of this week’s special Trade Deadline Edition of All Ball.

https://art19.com/shows/the-distraction/episodes/d0e962b6-9e05-45c6-af98-0b5f8d111e53

articles.author: Ray Ratto
articles.description:
Under any other circumstances, in any other year, Kirk Cousins being traded back to the Minnesota Vikings would be universally mocked under the You Can't Make Someone Go Back Home statutes. The story of Kirk and the Vikes is one that had been told all the way through, in no great rush at that, and was on the merits not one that would have had the public demanding or even imagining a reboot. But here, now, in the situation in which the Vikings have placed themselves—well, put it this way: No NFL trade has ever had so many people call their shot ahead of time and then nod with approval after it came to pass.
Yes, even though Cousins already titillated and frustrated the Vikings alternately over six years by being Almost That Guy, they brought him back on Tuesday in a desperate admission that they had turned their quarterback room into a lividly radioactive dump site. Cousins, we must presume, went with a song in his heart, because he finally found his nirvana: a place without a young quarterback desperate to make his bones waiting to replace him.
A Cousins trade of some kind had been rumored from the moment he landed in Las Vegas to play for the Raiders, primarily because he was so obviously there to hold the place card until No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza was ready to replace him. Minnesota wasn't much of a trade option until the Vikings made themselves one—well, the only one. After Cousins was lured to Atlanta (illegally, as the league eventually ruled), the Vikings fell in and out of love with J.J. McCarthy, fell briefly in like with Kyler Murray and then watched his hamstring explode, watched Carson Wentz melt into a puddle in real time on Monday night, and rejected Max Brosmer as a viable option on the fly.
articles.title: Look Who Came Crawling Back To Kirk Cousins

articles.description:
The Capitals beat the Senators in overtime on Tuesday, but the most impactful play of the night was not a goal. Late in the third, with the score 2-2, Ottawa's Nick Cousins kind of casually gathered the puck in his own corner and started to skate up the ice. Before he could do anything with it, however, Cousins got comprehensively bulldozed by Caps defenseman Jakob Chychrun, who sent his opponent's body into horizontal flight against the boards before it bounced limply to the ice. After a review, the refs deemed the hit clean, but Cousins did not return to action. He didn't go to the hospital, but according to his coach Travis Green, "He’s not doing great.”

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=g3E6wjvAA9M


I have complicated thoughts about this play. It is very difficult for me to resist marveling at Chychrun's spectacular force and its devastating aftermath; it's as real an athletic feat as any skillful dangle. The fact that it was perpetrated on Cousins, a pest so annoying that his peers named him the league's most punchable player last year, only makes it easier to ignore the human toll. But it's also hard for me to see it and not think about Claude Lemieux, among other ex-NHL tough guys, whose brain was donated to CTE research after his death by suicide earlier this year.
articles.title: Nick Cousins Sure As Hell Was “Not Doing Great”

articles.author: Tom Ley
articles.description:
The weightlessness of the early season and the ever-increasing rate of injuries can make it hard to sell a weeknight NBA game in November. There remains, however, a reliable shortcut between "box score I'll check in the morning" and "game I gotta watch live," and it is a route lined with beef. 
Beef was not promised in the leadup to Tuesday night's game between the Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers, which pit former teammates Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum against each other for the first time since Brown was traded in the offseason, but a savory aroma was in the air. Brown's trade brought with it all sorts of thinly sourced reports about he and Tatum having a contentious relationship, and those suspicions were more or less confirmed a few weeks ago. On Oct. 22, Tatum posted on YouTube another episode of his self-produced documentary series. A clip of this episode, in which Tatum recounts the shock he felt when he found out that Brown had been traded—"You traded him down the street?" he says to the person who broke the news—was posted on Instagram, and in the comments section of that post, Brown responded with the "cap" emoji.
Brown was calling Tatum a liar, which was enough to elicit some direct questions about their relationship from reporters. ​"Jayson's a great guy," Brown said. "Like I said, great family, hell of a basketball player, hell of a PR team. There's no beef, but it might be a little lamb chops, and some gravy, you know what I mean? He should stay ready at all times."
articles.title: Jayson Tatum And Jaylen Brown’s Beef Is Severely Undercooked

articles.author: Chris Thompson
articles.description:
Here is a thing that Republicans do not do when they sweep into power: They do not bother brainstorming ways that they can signal a values match with the people who oppose them, and whom they have just defeated. They do not look around, blinking, from the hilltop they have just won, and fret about appealing to the vanquished foes lying half-dead at their feet. When Republicans win, they set about changing the laws, or using the existing laws to their advantage. That is the job. Republican lawmakers express their values through the laws that they make and enforce. They do not get sidetracked by the idea that they can make friends with progressives, and not only because they know that their voters do not want them to do that. They perceive an authentic mismatch of values, and their solution to that is to make progressives eat shit.
You will say that this is a weakness of their politics. You will point to their long-dwindling popularity and last week's electoral bloodbath, and say that their reflexive and idiotic tribalism is a terminal illness, and that Democrats should learn from it only that it is self-defeating. You fool. Here you have done them the favor of flattening the actual, substantive, qualitative differences between the goals of the right and the left.
You shouldn't do that, because those differences are important. People on the left want things—actual tangible things: laws and institutions and structures—that make sense, that arise from active, curious, engaged minds thinking deeply about how to run a community of any size or complexity. Those things are aimed at the goal of making society more equitable and less brutal, and making life more dignified and less degrading.

articles.description:
Yesterday, good internet friend Baldur Bjarnason shared a series of shorts he made on why he doesn’t use generative AI, and it got me thinking about how much of my career has spent being against things.
Early in my career, I was for web performance and accessibility and building cool things.
But as JavaScript frameworks became increasingly ubiquitous, we saw the things I was for start to degrade rapidly. Sites got slower and harder to use.
articles.title: For and against
